item.text:
**3B.1 Research Note: Bongbong Marcos in 2024**

**Working judgment:** `Mostly no`. Marcos-era institutions took a few protective or accountability-oriented steps, but the 2024 record still shows continued extrajudicial killings, disappearances, torture/ill-treatment, arbitrary detention, and weak accountability. The strongest positive evidence is indirect or institutional; the strongest negative evidence is broader and more concrete.

| Direction | Title | Publisher | Date | URL | Claim-level summary | Question IDs |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|---|---|
| Positive | 2024 Country Reports on Human Rights Practices: Philippines | U.S. Department of State | 2024 | https://www.ecoi.net/en/document/2128580.html | The report says the Marcos administration refocused the antidrug campaign toward treatment, due process, and rule-of-law-based investigations, which is the clearest official-signaled shift away from Duterte-style arbitrary violence. | 3B.1 |
| Positive | Marcos bans POGOs, cites disorder it caused PH | Philippine Daily Inquirer | 2024-07-23 | https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/1964063/marcos-bans-pogo-cites-disorder-it-caused-ph | Marcos banned all POGOs after citing torture, kidnapping, human trafficking, and murder linked to the industry. This is a real protective step against severe abuse, though it is more about criminal exploitation than state violence. | 3B.1 |
| Positive | Marcos announces ban on all POGO | GMA News Online | 2024-07-22 | https://www.gmanetwork.com/news/topstories/nation/914272/marcos-announces-ban-on-all-pogo/story/ | Marcos framed the ban as stopping “grave abuse” and illegal acts, and ordered POGOs wound down by year-end. This supports a limited claim that he acted against a violent abuse network. | 3B.1 |
| Positive | DOJ creates task force to review EJK cases | Philippine News Agency | 2024-11-06 | https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1237266 | The DOJ created a task force to investigate Duterte-era extrajudicial killings, build cases, and file charges if warranted. That is the strongest 2024 accountability move tied to state violence. | 3B.1 |
| Positive | No PH cooperation with ICC unless PRRD wants it – PBBM | Presidential Communications Office | 2024-11-14 | https://pco.gov.ph/news_releases/no-ph-cooperation-with-icc-unless-prrd-wants-it-pbbm/ | Marcos said domestic authorities would keep reviewing the drug-war record and the DOJ would continue reassessing testimonies and evidence. This is some accountability signaling, but it is narrowed by his refusal to cooperate with the ICC. | 3B.1 |
| Negative | World Report 2025: Philippines | Human Rights Watch | 2025-01-16 | https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2025/country-chapters/philippines | HRW says drug-war killings persisted in 2024, enforced disappearances continued, and the Marcos administration still refused to cooperate with the ICC. This is the strongest high-level negative assessment of the year. | 3B.1 |
| Negative | 2024 Country Reports on Human Rights Practices: Philippines | U.S. Department of State | 2024 | https://www.ecoi.net/en/document/2128580.html | The report lists credible reports of arbitrary or unlawful killings, disappearances, torture, arbitrary arrest or detention, and serious abuses in conflict. It also says police/security-force abuse remained a serious issue. | 3B.1 |
| Negative | Philippines: “Submit and surrender”: the harms of arbitrary drug detention in the Philippines | Amnesty International | 2024-11-28 | https://www.amnesty.org/en/documents/asa35/8759/2024/en/ | Amnesty documents arbitrary detention in drug “treatment and rehabilitation” centers, including torture, ill-treatment, and forced or unreliable confessions. This undercuts any claim that residents were broadly protected from abusive state or state-linked custody practices. | 3B.1 |
| Negative | World Report 2024: Philippines | Human Rights Watch | 2024 | https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/philippines | HRW says Marcos’s rhetoric was more measured than Duterte’s, but the state still failed to protect activists, and abuses such as killings, disappearances, and criminalization of critics continued. It also notes the government invited UN experts, which is a partial positive but not a resolution. | 3B.1 |
| Negative | Philippines | Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism | 2024-06-17 | https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/digital-news-report/2024/philippines | The report notes red-tagging, libel pressure, blocked sites, and continuing threats against journalists under Marcos. This is relevant because it shows intimidation and coercive pressure remained part of the civic environment. | 3B.1 |

**Synthesis**
- Marcos did take some protective steps in 2024, especially the POGO ban and the DOJ task force on drug-war killings.
- Those actions were limited and largely reactive.
- The balance of independent reporting says serious abuses persisted: drug-related killings, disappearances, torture, arbitrary detention, and intimidation of critics.
- I found no strong 2024 evidence that Marcos personally accepted responsibility for these abuses or built a durable protection system that clearly reversed inherited patterns.

**Search gap**
- I did not find solid 2024 evidence of a broad, president-led reform package ending arbitrary detention, torture, disappearances, or political imprisonment.
- The positive record is mostly indirect, institutional, or limited to specific sectors, while the negative record is broader and better documented.
